utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. I think despite the fact that there are some minor issues pending, we'll first continue with the witness. Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Perhaps I meanwhile with deal with one of them. The Prosecution has informed the parties that it has discovered an error in the English translation of P2900 which was admitted through Ewan Brown on the 12th of December of last year. Several pages were in incorrect order and also several pages were missing. The corrected English translation that is been uploaded into e-court under doc ID B003-2526-1ET.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I take it that you'd like to have the original document be replaced by the new one?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, you're hereby instructed to replace the existing document under P2900 by the new one of which I just read out the number. Mr. Lukic, if there's any problems, within 48 hours we'd like to hear from you. Then good morning, Mr. Davidovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, I'd first like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration that you've given at the begin of your testimony. Mr. Jeremy will now continue his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And before we do so. May I urge the parties that in view of the assessment of the next witness and in view of the fact that we are not sitting next week that we do our utmost best to see that we can conclude the evidence of the next witness today. Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Davidovic.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, in your statement, you discuss Betonjerka prison and I'd like to start today by discussing that in a little bit more detail with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we please see paragraph 32 of your statement D675 on the screen. And if we could go to page 8 in the English and page 10 in the B/C/S, please. There we are.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Davidovic, in paragraph 32, referring to Betonjerka prison, you -- midway down that paragraph, you say: "As I have already stated, it was not the military that brought these people in. That was within the purview of the police." Now, here you're referring to captured persons being brought in to Betonjerka prison; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, these were persons captured during the mop-up operations that you were involved in in late May, early June; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So are you saying that persons who you dealt with during the mop-up operations in Hrustovo and Vrhpolje, no persons from those villages were -- were brought into Betonjerka prison; is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The persons that I had contact with were not taken there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: I accept that the -- you say the persons that you had contact with were not taken there, but are you aware that persons were taken there from Vrhpolje and Hrustovo during the mop-up operations that you were involved in?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since I was only a commander of one battalion, and there were a number of units, I don't know about those other units. Now, as the commander of my battalion and my subordinates, I know that they never arrested anyone, nor did they bring anyone to the Betonjerka prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, in paragraph 32 of your statement, and I've read out the quote, you don't limit your evidence to your own battalion. You say that it was not the military that brought these people in; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what I believed, and I didn't have different information. In addition, we had no order to detain --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, I'll stop you there. Your statement reads: "As I have already stated, it was not the military that brought those people in." I now do understand that that is what you believe, although your statement doesn't say "I believe that," but your statement says they were not brought in by the military. You tell us now that what happened in other units you are not aware of. Therefore, I take it that you're also not aware of whether they were taken, the captured persons were taken to Betonjerka. Is that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't speak about other units, but about myself and my unit, I can claim --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We leave it to that. You can't say anything about that. So therefore your statement that they were not brought in by the military is a statement which expresses your belief, not knowledge of facts. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I may just also ask a question. Mr. Davidovic, at page 3, line 1, Mr. Jeremy asked you the question: "Now, here you're referring to captured persons being brought in to Betonjerka prison; correct?" And you said: "Yes." My question to you is by whom were these people captured?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To the best of my knowledge, the majority of the people who were brought there were taken in by the public security services of the security service centre in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's not my question. I'm not saying who brought them in, I said who captured them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't know. I suppose that they interviewed them there on the spot. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. You don't know. Mr. Jeremy, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Could we look at an exhibit in connection with this topic and it's P2900, which is the exhibit that we've just corrected. Now the correction means that our pages are thrown out slightly but we are dealing with that. Could we please see page 14 in the English and page 18 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, while that's being brought up, the chief of the Sanski Most public security station was Mirko Vrucinic; correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremy, I do understand that although I instructed the Registry to replace the old one by the new one that it has not been completed yet, so that it's still the old one at this moment we are working with. And perhaps since you're now questioning the witness about P2900, that you later in one way or another guide us through where we have to find what you refer to now in that new version.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'll do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: In which case could we please see page 2 of P2900 in the English and page 8 -- we've got the correct page in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Davidovic, we see that this is a report of the Sanski Most SJB and it's dated the 18th of August, 1992. And it's sent to the National Security Service of the CSB.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we go to page 4 in the English, please, and page 21 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And we see there that it is signed by the chief of the SJB Mirko Vrucinic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Can we please go back to page 2 in the English and 18 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Davidovic, we see at the top of the text, typed text, the existence of collection and investigation centres in the municipality. In the first paragraph, we read that during the time of the armed conflict, two collection and investigation centres were set up in Sanski Most. And in the next sentence, Betonjerka is mentioned. Now, the next paragraph deals specifically with the setting up of that facility. I'd like to go to the third paragraph and ask you to focus on that. And in particular, the first sentence. There we read: "Most of the persons, about 90 per cent, were brought in by the army as prisoners from the zones where there had been fighting." In the next paragraph --

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And we'll need to go to the next page in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: -- we read: "The army brought in prisoners from the zones in which combat operations had taken place in trucks and buses, housed them in the facilities mentioned (the centres) but do not make lists of the persons brought in. Persons were brought in by the army in the standard manner by patrols and detention orders." Now, Mr. Davidovic, you would agree that the chief of the Sanski Most security centre would have known whether or not it was the army that was bringing in prisoners to Betonjerka prison?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you allow me, I can tell you that I really don't know about this. Maybe Mirko Vrucinic counted as part of the army Territorial Defence who were also uniformed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, what may be have been the case is not something we invite you to speak about. What you know, you can tell us. Mr. Jeremy, the document was put to the witness in which it clearly states that at least the army was bringing in prisoners to the detention facilities. The witness says he doesn't know about it. Therefore, let's leave it to that and we cannot -- we don't have the benefit of the knowledge of the witness to further assist the Chamber in this respect. Meanwhile, by the way, the new version of P2900 is in e-court so if you would like to use that version, you have an opportunity to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm moving away from this document now but I will follow up with the relevant page number corrections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There are not many, I believe. Yes. Now, that's fine. If there's no change in the page numbering you're referring to, because you took us to the cover page, to the signature page, and then to page 2. If page 2 is still page 2, then there's no need to further explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: In fact, the cover page is now page 14. The signature page is page 16, and the second page I moved to is page 15 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. That's hereby on the record then. Please proceed. There's no need to further explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Davidovic, I'd like to go back to paragraph 32 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we put that on the screen, please, D675.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, in the final two sentences of paragraph 32, you state: "Also, the military did not send detainees to Manjaca nor did it secure these convoys. All that was within the purview of civilian authorities." Now, in connection with this part of your statement, I'd like to show you another document. That's P2409.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps, Mr. Jeremy, the first question for the witness would be do you believe that the army did not secure these convoys and that they did not send detainees to Manjaca or do you know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that my unit never sent or escorted anyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So therefore, do I understand you clearly that you do not know whether other units, other army units sent people to Manjaca and were involved in the -- in escorting the convoys, to secure the convoys?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Based on the information that I had, members of the 6th Sanska Infantry Brigade never took anyone to Manjaca nor had they escorted anyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, first of all, that's not what your statement says but it's hereby then corrected that it was not your unit and that on the basis of your information other units neither did it, and what your information is remains totally unclear. Mr. Jeremy, if you put the document to the witness, we could keep it pretty short, I would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, what is the basis of your knowledge for saying that units -- other units of the 6th Sanska Infantry Brigade did not send prisoners to Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I learned that at the meetings with the brigade command and the Chief of Staff, and it was never mentioned that any of our members or our units sent anyone to Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Were you familiar with Colonel Stevilovic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: If I told you he was the assistant commander for intelligence and security in the 1st Krajina Corps, would that refresh your memory?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Let's take a look at P2409, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Davidovic, we see that this is a document dated the 4th of June, 1992, and we see that these are conclusions of the Crisis Staff of the Serbian municipality of Sanski Most from a session held on the 4th of June, 1992. We see they adopted the following conclusions, and I'd like to focus on the first. We read, number one: "Mirko Vrucinic, Nedjelko Rasula, and Colonel Nedo Anicic shall be in charge of resolving the issue of prisoners and their categorisation and deportation to Manjaca. The first category, politicians; second category, national extremists; third category, people unwelcome in Sanski Most municipality. "In view of this have a talk with Colonel Stevilovic from the 1st Krajina Corps." Now, Mr. Davidovic, this document is dated the 4th of June 1992. That's immediately after the mop-up operations that the 6th Brigade were involved in in Mahala, Vrhpolje and Hrustovo; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Davidovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jeremy. Any questions in redirect?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a few one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'll stay with the same document. If we can have it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Davidovic, good morning once again.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff of the Serbian municipality of Sanski Most, according to you and to the best of your knowledge, was it able to issue any orders to an officer belonging to the 1st Krajina Corps?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the spirit of our language, the sentence that was read out to you, to the effect that talks should be held with Colonel Stevilovic, is that the future tense?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. To hold talks means in the future.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that the Manjaca facility was under the jurisdiction of the corps?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we have any confusion, you asked the witness what have talks would mean, meaning in the future. My understanding of the English language doesn't bring me any other interpretation, but I'm also looking at the Prosecution in view of this, have a talk with means engage in a conversation still to be held. So I was puzzled by why you referred to your language where at least the English, as far as I can see, raises no doubts as to the meaning of this to be in the future.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, at least then I was not puzzled, the only one, actually, puzzled by this line of questions because the line of questions was whether your unit ever transported prisoners to Manjaca and I don't know what we got from this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, only that they discussed, they discussed prisoners in three categories and that they -- it was intended that someone would talk to Mr. Stevilovic, that's the only thing I think we get from this document, exclusively this document. The context in which it was presented, of course, is a different matter and whether other evidence sheds more or a different light on what we read here.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Before I continue with my cross-examination I just want to say, because we have to save time today, and -- topic with the Colonel Basara, whether he was a member of the Crisis Staff or not, I think is better to discuss with Colonel Basara who is going to testify in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I leave it to you whether you consider it. I think we will do well within the time estimates we made today, and I am surprised that you say you're going to cross-examine the witness. That's at least how it was translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Redirect, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Redirect, yes. I don't know what the testimony of that witness will bring us, so if you think that it's of any use to also ask this witness about, but first of all whether he has any knowledge of it which is not the same as whether he has any beliefs in it, then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You were shown -- or rather on page 2654 -- 26514 from line 10 onwards, that's on yesterday's transcript, you were asked whether you co-ordinated your actions with the Territorial Defence and public security when you guarded facilities. We are talking about the 20th of April, 1992. On the 20th of April, who headed the Territorial Defence in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Nedjelko Anicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And the public security centre?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mirko Vrucinic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did the military issue orders to the Territorial Defence in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I suppose that it didn't, but did it issue orders to the public security centre?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just briefly, based on what you know about the Crisis Staff, you sometimes attended meetings of the Crisis Staff instead of Basara, you told us that. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What did Colonel Basara tell you when he asked you to go in his stead? Did he tell you that you could vote on his behalf?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I couldn't vote.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. So you couldn't. Did he tell you that he had the right of vote when decisions were made by the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He told us that he was not a member of the Crisis Staff but that he occasionally attended the meetings of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yesterday on transcript page - I'm moving on to another topic - 26532, you were shown P2502.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's under seal because it's the statement of the witness. RM708.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Yeah, that was my mistake. It's not under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Oh no, okay. So I'm just referencing the document. We don't even have to have it on our screens. But -- now we have it, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yesterday, you told us about Hrustovo and the death of the three fighters who were moving in the direction of Hrustovo. Had an ultimatum been given before the military started moving in the direction of Hrustovo?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was an announcement that looked like an ultimatum, but it was a request more than anything else. It was addressed that all the people who had weapons, asking them to hand them over to avoid combat, to avoid fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were civilians mentioned in that request?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Civilians were not mentioned. The only thing that was requested was for the weapons to be handed over.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: After that, after that request demand, ultimatum, whatever you want to call it, what happened to the civilians in Hrustovo?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you will allow me, I'd like to tell you about the conversation with the representative of the village whom I invited to talk to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We have that in your statement. Do you know what happened to the civilians? Did they stay? Did they leave? What do you know about the civilians in Hrustovo?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Apart from what I stated in the statement and the case that I mentioned and that I witnessed, I have no other information. That's all I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Davidovic. That's all we had for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, do you have any questions, Mr. Jeremy? But I would have one or two questions first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, that ultimatum was addressed to whom?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the villagers of Hrustovo and Vrhpolje who were there and others who were staying with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was the -- were these villages mainly populated by Muslims?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, one could say a hundred per cent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To whom did they have to render their weapons?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were supposed to hand over their weapons either to us, the military, or to the public security centre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And when you say the military, exactly when was it in time? Just before early June, is that, late May?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was sometime in May -- in April, the end of April, the beginning of May. I don't know exactly. It's in my statement. I can't remember as I sit here today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So that's still during the JNA time, if I could say so.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact date when the JNA became the VRS, when that changed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then we leave it to that. Was an ultimatum sent to Serb villages as well?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any reason why they did not receive such an ultimatum?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because the majority Serbian population, i.e., able-bodied men, had responded to the call-ups and they joined various units, and thus they received weapons legally and used them for various activities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But there were Serbs who were not in the army, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were such people. They also had weapons. I suppose that they guarded them to protect themselves because the unit was not always deployed in the territory of Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So if I understand you well, that the Serbs were allowed, those who were not members of the army, were allowed to keep their weapons to defend themselves, whereas the Muslims were -- were sent an ultimatum that they should render the weapons because you thought they would use them for other purposes. Is that well understood?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as a matter of fact, yes, but there weren't many, as far as I know, but I can't really talk about everything with full certainty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, you've been in that area for that period of time. Could you tell us the end result as far as casualties are concerned. Could you give us any idea about how many Serbs, approximately, died as a consequence of combat, crimes being executed, whatever, and how many Muslims were finally killed either in combat or by criminal activities during that relatively short period of time, let's say, after the -- well, let's say in the month May, June, after the ultimatums.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. I don't know it for a fact. I know that throughout the war, 472 men in my brigade got killed, over 2.000 were wounded. And as for the entire area throughout the period that you have mentioned, I really don't know. I don't want to make a mistake if I tell you anything. And if you will allow me, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please. In your brigade, there were -- all those who were -- got killed, were they Serbs or were they persons of another ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think -- actually, I know for a fact that one of them was a Muslim, but he died of natural causes. I believe that there were one or two cases of people who got killed and who were not Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, I do understand from your answer that you do not know how many Muslims were killed during that period. This Chamber has received some evidence about Muslims being killed and evidence which I think yesterday you questioned whether it was accurate or not, but apart from that, do you know anything about numbers of Muslims killed either in combat or through criminal activity of persons carrying weapons? Whether it's a crime or whether you call it combat I'm not that much interested in it. But do you have any idea about the number of Muslims that got killed?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I can only tell you what I heard. I don't have an idea of my own. I apologise, may I just say that I'm really sorry for all the victims, but it happened. It just happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, whether it just happened is further to be considered. Tell us what you heard about the number of Muslims that got killed in Sanski Most. How many did you hear?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Throughout all that time, according to what I heard, some 200 or so were killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremy, any further questions for the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, you were shown a document dated the 4th of June 1992, and this is a document that related to the categorisation of prisoners to be taken to Manjaca and there's a reference to the consultation with Colonel Stevilovic. You recall that, yes? Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Where does the document say that they had to be taken to Manjaca? Could I just have a look at it again?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Certainly. Could we look at P2409.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You'll forgive me that I don't have a ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So just in the first sentence, number one, you see --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, yes, I see it. Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... persons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, let me see. One second. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: There's a reference to categorisation and the deportation to Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please. Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, you were asked whether the language suggested that this was a conversation to be had in the future and you agreed that it was. Now, in connection with that I'd like to show you a follow-up document --

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And that's P3255. Could we have that on our screens, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, we see that this is a document. It's dated the 6th of June, 1992. It's from the public security station Sanski Most. It's signed Acting Chief of Police Security Station, Mirko Vrucinic. I'd like to refer your attention to the first paragraph where we read: "In accordance with the agreement reached with the Banja Luka corps command (Colonel Stevilovic) and the chief of the police department of the Banja Luka Security Services Centre, Stevo Markovic, we are sending you a group of persons who were captured during combat operations in the municipality of Sanski Most as well as the persons who co-operated with them in the course of preparations for an armed uprising in the municipality of Sanski Most." Mr. Davidovic, you would agree that this appears a conversation was indeed had with Mr. Stevilovic and he was involved in the transportation of these prisoners to Manjaca camp; yes?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to say that Manjaca was a military facility from before. That facility belonged to the military. Who did what during the war, I don't know. All I know that before the war, it was already a designated military facility.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, just one final question. You refer to casualties in your unit and in your statement you refer to four documents that contain details of the wounding and death of members of your unit. I just want to clarify that these wounding and these deaths occurred in September and October 1995; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we can see it in the document, that that's that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just short one regarding these documents. My --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, it's usually -- you have called the witness, cross-examined --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- re-examined, further cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I kindly ask you just to explain why he mentioned those documents from 1995, if you can ask him that, because of the position he held at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I asked about early 1992 so I now understood, irrespective of what the reasons may have been, that he referred to numbers which are of 1995 and therefore has not answered my question. That's -- he may have had good reasons for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] His statement is in regard to 1992 but these documents are from 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. We'll carefully look at them and then the witness may have had his reasons to refer to those documents. We leave it to that. Mr. Davidovic, this concludes your testimony in this Court. I'd like to thank you very much for coming to The Hague and for having answered all the questions that were put to you either by the Defence or by the Prosecution or by the Bench and I wish you a safe return home again. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, just one question for Mr. Lukic. He --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: He didn't tender the associated exhibits. I'm not sure if you were planning to.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I thought we'll deal with that during the administrative proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We don't need the witness for that, I take it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps can we use the remaining five minutes for associated exhibits with this witness. Let's have a look at this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I spoke with my learned friend yesterday and I was informed that they might object to the first associated exhibits aside from the statement. It's 1D20348.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you just give me a second of time. Let's see what we have. We have the -- first of all, we have the statement, the second one is pending translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's why I said Prosecution, as I understood them, intends to object it. That translation was supposed to be finalised yesterday. But I checked in this morning, it has not been translated yet. So we would just propose that to be MFI'd.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Any objection against it being MFI'd, Mr. Jeremy?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, but it's an extract of a larger document so I would like to reserve the right to perhaps add in additional excerpts if we feel they provide you with additional context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do see that Mr. Lukic does not oppose that suggestion. Therefore, Madam Registrar, 1D02034a would receive number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D676, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Marked for identification. Then I move through the list. 1D03069 would receive number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Number D677, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence. 1D03448.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Number D678.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted. 1D03449.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Number D679, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted. 1D03450.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Number D680, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence. If --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And that's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's it because all the other documents referred to are already in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then I'd like to briefly, because we have two minutes left, deal with the other documents which are still pending. I do understand that two revised English translations were received by the Prosecution, that they were uploaded into e-court, and I'll deal with each of the two. For P4971, the newly uploaded English translation in e-court is known under doc ID 0082-0954-1. Madam Registrar, you are hereby instructed to replace the old English translation by the new one. I now come to P5023. The new version of the English translation has been uploaded into e-court under doc ID 0607-1691-1. Madam Registrar, you are hereby instructed to replace the current English translation with the new one uploaded under number I just mentioned. I think that deals with the -- those administrative matters. None other pending at this moment. And, Mr. Jeremy, I see that Ms. Stewart is hiding behind a column, but if she confirms even only by nodding that I've dealt with all the pending issues in this respect. Then we can take a break. Is the Defence ready to call the next witness after the break?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, we are, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that's no protective measures for Mr. Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No protective measures, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Half an hour, 45 minutes for the Prosecution as matters stand now. We take the break and we resume at ten minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll wait for the witness to be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration. The text is handed out to you and I'd like to invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly swear that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated, Mr. Petkovic. Mr. Petkovic, you'll first be examined by Mr. Stojanovic. You find him to your left. Mr. Stojanovic is counsel for Mr. Mladic. Please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning to you, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please state your full name for the record but slowly.

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Svetozar, father's name Ilija, Petkovic, born on 27th January, 1947, in the former Republic of Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Petkovic, have you given a statement to General Mladic's Defence team about the events in Foca in writing?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can we have in e-court document 65 ter 1D01693.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Petkovic, you can see in front of you -- this is your first appearance before this Court?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I would kindly ask you to look in front of you on the screen. There's a statement there and I'm asking you to tell me whether this is your signature on this page?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have signed it in front of your colleagues who interviewed me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at the last page of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Is this your signature as well on the last page of this document as well as the date when you signed it? Did you write it with your own hand?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is the date when they came and I signed confirming the veracity of the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I were, after you have given the solemn declaration, to put the same questions to you, would you confirm once again that everything contained in this statement is truthful?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR PETKOVIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't change anything that has been recorded and I can confirm that it reflects everything I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to tender the witness's statement, the statement of Svetozar Petkovic, 65 ter 1D01693.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D1693 receives number D681, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D681 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic. If you either by reading a summary of this statement and if you have any further questions for the witness, to put them to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. With your leave, I'm going to read the summary of Petkovic Svetozar's statement. When the war broke out, he was a teacher at the secondary school in Foca. As of 1993, he was a teacher at the faculty of dentistry. Following the outbreak of war in Foca, he was tasked with the Crisis Staff to provide food supplies and equipment supplies for the population and the units stationed in Foca. At the moment when first major armed conflicts broke out in the town itself on the 8th and 9th April, 1992, misinformation was broadcast in the media about the arrival of 5.000 Chetniks from Montenegro which triggered the events in which the majority of the Muslim population being afraid decided to leave the town. In April, May, and June of 1992, there were armed groups and individuals in Foca municipality who were not under a single command so that there was complete lawlessness there. The Crisis Staff was unable and didn't have the strength to stop the self-will of these groups and the self-proclaimed commanders. For several months following the liberation of Foca, the town was cut off from the military and civilian authorities beyond Foca. He has personal knowledge of the fact that towards the end of June 1992, a first group of JNA officers arrived in Foca who placed themselves at the disposal of the Crisis Staff of Foca. In early June -- in early July or late June, a brigade was established. The witness was tasked with the duty of the headquarters commander as well as the task of being involved in humanitarian activities to serve the needs of the population of Foca regardless of their ethnicity. He witnessed, himself, the confrontation between the VRS command and various paramilitary groups in an attempt to place them within the system of singleness of command and subordination. He states that Marko Kovac, as the commander of a military unit in Foca, throughout the whole 1992 failed to completely disband these units and oust them from Foca municipality. With your leave, Your Honours, I would only put a couple of questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Can we please have in e-court paragraph 3 of the document D681 which is the witness statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Petkovic, my question is the following: In your statement, you spoke about dissemination of misinformation on the radio. Can you tell the Chamber, were you in a position to hear this misinformation?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I was driving in a vehicle where we, as usual, were listening to Radio Sarajevo. At one point, journalist Semso Tockakovic announced on Radio Sarajevo that 5.000 armed Chetniks from Montenegro were coming to Foca.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. You are now telling us what you heard on the radio. Now that already appears in your statement. The question was put to you whether you could hear that on the radio and you said you were listening to the radio driving in a car. Now, I don't know whether there would be much dispute about if there is a public broadcast, that everyone who has a radio or a car with a radio in it, whatever, can listen to that. So the relevant information is has the witness heard it by his own ears and he says yes, and that's what I take it from the statement as well. So let's try to be concise. And, Mr. Stojanovic, try to keep the witness with your question and don't ask any questions on obvious matters. And don't seek repetition of what is already in the statement. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 7 of your statement --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And can we please focus our attention on paragraph 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: -- about the fact that towards the end of June or in early July 1992, a brigade in Preljuca was officially established. Can you please tell the Chamber according to what you know, prior to the establishment of the brigade was in charge of the combat and the units of Territorial Defence in Foca?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Prior to that was Miroslav Stanic, the commander of the Crisis Staff, who held all the reins in his hands. There were, though, a lot of paramilitary units that were more or less involved in plundering, expulsion of people, so there were no organised units of territorial and military district, so whoever had any kind of weapon became involved. There was no proper command that would lead us in the right direction and follow orders so that we can perform the tasks in the best possible way.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going to finish with the following question. When you say in paragraph 8 of your statement that you were sure that Marko Kovac as the commander failed to fully disband those units, what is the basis of that claim in your statement when you say that you were sure of that?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR PETKOVIC
utterances.text: I was present on several occasions when he tried to communicate with those paramilitary units, however, they completely ignored him. I was also present when one of the citizens and a person from the former Serbia was running a store selling TV sets and furniture. He was supposed to transport these goods to Serbia, but this self-proclaimed commander of a paramilitary unit by the name of Pero Elez seized this truck trailer with all the goods, and I was present in the command headquarters when this man came to Marko Kovac seeking his assistance to have his commodities returned to him because they had requested 5.000 German marks to return it to him. Marko advised him neither to try to get the goods and not to give them any money because even if he gave them the money, they were going to kill him. That led me to conclude that Marko was totally incapable of dealing with these units or issuing any orders to them. In addition to that, I was present all the time while these paramilitary units were there. Marko was in charge of a long front line where combatants were deployed, while at the same time these paramilitary units were loitering around the town and plundering. I heard a lot of bad things about them although I was not always present, but I do know that they were looting.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Petkovic, thank you for your answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we have no questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stojanovic. Ms. MacGregor, are you ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. I am ready. If you can just give me a moment to set up my stand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Petkovic, you will be cross-examined by Ms. MacGregor. You'll find her to your right. Ms. MacGregor is counsel for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: In your statement, you mention Miro Stanic, head of the Crisis Staff. Did you know him personally?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR PETKOVIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Did you know Petko Cancar, the mayor of Foca personally?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR PETKOVIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Did you know Vojislav Maksimovic, an SDS politician in Foca? Did you know him personally?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, personally.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And Velibor Ostojic, the minister of information. Did you personally know him?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR PETKOVIC
utterances.text: I knew him as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Can the Prosecution please have 65 ter 03579.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Mr. Petkovic, you'll see on your screen I'm bringing up a transcript of a broadcast on Belgrade Radio from 14 April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And if we can focus on the first couple paragraphs on the English version so that they're a bit larger, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Now, you can see in parentheses near the top, it says, "Velibor Ostojic report from Foca." Now, I'm going to read from the transcript of the broadcast. "Fighting has continued in Foca today. It is fierce and climaxed at around 1500 when Serbian territorials wanted to liberate the residents from one of the most conspicuous skyscrapers in Donje Polje which the party of democratic action fighters had turned into a veritable bunker of sniper nests. A fierce battle then flared up in which all weapons were used." Is the reference to Serbian territorials a reference to the Serbian Territorial Defence? Mr. Petkovic, do you need me to repeat my question? I believe you do. The reference in this broadcast to the Serbian Territorials, do you understand that as a reference to the Serbian Territorial Defence in Foca?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I suppose so. It was not an organised unit. It was not a special unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Now if we move on to the question posed by the announcer, it says: "So, if we understand you, one side does not control Foca but fighting is continuing." Ostojic answers: "The Serbian Territorial Defence is controlling a huge part of the town. They are particularly in control of the wide area of the commune. The entire Territorial Defence is the Foca commune is on its feet." Is the description Ostojic provides of the situation in Foca consistent with your recollection of events around April 14, 1992?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Things developed more or less in that way, but I didn't know whether that was called a Territorial Defence because I know that it was all in a very unorganised manner. No specialty was taken into account when we were engaged in our units, and we were engaged in various parts of the territory. I don't know whether these units were called the Territorial Defence or not. I know that the Crisis Staff was in charge headed by --

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Mr. Petkovic, we're trying to finish your testimony today so that you don't have to stay in The Hague for an extended period. If you can please answer the questions just as I've asked them. Now, at least as of April 14th, 1992, would you agree that it appears that Ostojic was able to communicate news about Foca to the outside world?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR PETKOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, he was not in that position. Telephone lines were down until the moment somebody came to help us establish communication with Tornik in Serbia, so we could at least communicate with the command on Velecevo which was headquartered in the former female prison.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Around 14 April 1992, were you personally meeting with Velibor Ostojic for -- with any frequency?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR PETKOVIC
utterances.text: I was always in the Crisis Staff. Velibor Ostojic was not a member but he was always there. Vojislav Maksimovic and Petko Cancar were also not a member of the Crisis Staff but they attended the meetings. I was often there as well and I often saw him. He didn't spend much time in Foca; however, I even doubt that he was there until the date that you've mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. MacGregor, could I seek clarification. Witness, you said as far as you knew, Velibor Ostojic was not in that position when asked about the 14th of April, 1992, and his contact with the media at that moment. What did you refer to where you said he was not in that position? What position did you mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether we understood each other well. He was not a member of the Crisis Staff. In the former government he was the minister of information. I don't know whether he was able to send information and how he was able to do that if that was at all possible, but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You're not suggesting that he was not in Foca.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sure he was in Foca, but for a very brief period of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. MacGregor.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The Prosecution tenders 03579 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 3579 receives number P6810, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Can the Prosecution please have Exhibit P2824.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Mr. Petkovic, on your screen you will soon see a communication from Velibor Ostojic to the Serbian government in Sarajevo dated 30 April 1992. I'm going to ask you to look, it's a bit hard to see, at the top upper left corner of the page, first page. Now, are you able to see there the words "fax sender"?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR PETKOVIC
utterances.text: No. I don't see that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter is not sure that she understood the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please tell us whether you see in the fax header the words "fax sender" followed by what seems to be a telephone number.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I see.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you. And if we can -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you to take a moment to read the contents of the document. Are you able to see that on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR PETKOVIC
utterances.text: The Territorial Defence of the Foca is still making every effort in the Serbian Territorial Defence -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Sorry, you don't need to read it out loud. I just want to make sure you're able to read it to yourself. Were you able to read the document?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR PETKOVIC
utterances.text: I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Now, as of April 30th, 1992, it's correct that Ostojic is able to communicate to authorities outside of Foca about the conditions in Foca; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR PETKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure that communications were possible. There was no electricity and then electricity came from Montenegro. But I'm not sure that any communication was possible before the radio station was -- or radio set was installed. Montenegro is very close to Foca. I don't know whether they could send reports from there, whether it was possible to get to Montenegro -- it was possible to get there within one hour. And once they were there whether they were able to send reports from there, it is possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Can the Prosecution please have 65 ter 15186.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: The document that will soon be on your screen is a report on activities relating to organising judiciary institutions in Foca municipality. The document itself is not dated but I'll refer you to the first sentence of the document. It states: "The working group of the Ministry of Justice visited Foca on 24 and 25 June 1992 and held a meeting with the president of the executive board of Foca Municipal Assembly." I'll stop there. Now, it appears from this report that government representatives were able to travel to Foca and report back to civilian authorities; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR PETKOVIC
utterances.text: I know nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution tenders this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 15186 receives number P6811, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: During your testimony --

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps on the 24th or on the 25th of June, they could get to Foca via Montenegro. I'm sure of that. But I don't know whether they ever used that possibility, whether they ever came via that route.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you. During your testimony today around temporary transcript pages 28 and 29, you discussed an event where Pero Elez seized a truck trailer with electronics. Do you remember discussing that event today? Do you remember discussing that event?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Do you know the approximate date that that happened, that you witnessed that event?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR PETKOVIC
utterances.text: That happened sometime at the beginning of April or rather at the end of April or the beginning of May. That was at the very beginning of the war. It must have been in April or May. I can't remember the date. Or sometime before June, perhaps. It was a long time ago so I can't remember the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: To your knowledge, at some point did Pero Elez come under the control of Marko Kovac?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR PETKOVIC
utterances.text: He never obeyed Marko Kovac nor was Marko Kovac able to give him any orders. As far as I know, he was in charge of his own unit until the moment the brigade was set up and until the moment the tactical group was set up and then they all became members of the VRS. They were all incorporated into the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: So around what date would you mark that incorporation?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR PETKOVIC
utterances.text: 28th of June, as far as I can remember, because I was there when the first brigade was established on Preljuca. The tactical group was set up after that. As far as I know, and I don't know much about the command at the time because I was very often absent as I travelled to Serbia and Montenegro to fetch humanitarian aid, I was very often absent from the city, so I am not familiar with the details of the inception of the tactical group. I know that the tactical group was set up and was -- and Komo [phoen] Kamicak [phoen] and Cajnice [phoen] became its members. I'm not sure of all these units but this is more or less what I remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Can the Prosecution please see 65 ter 17405.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: I've asked for a document to be shown on your screen which is a certificate issued by the RS in Foca municipality in 2008. It's a certificate for Pero Elez establishing participation in the war based on data from official records in the armed forces of RS and of the former SFRY. The date range which you can see on the first line of the list, if you will, the date range is 6 April 1992 to December 10, 1992; correct? Do you see that date range?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR PETKOVIC
utterances.text: I can see the date. Many combatants were -- approved their military status as of the very beginning of the war. That's what was agreed as a matter of a convenience. I'm not surprised that Pero Elez also was among those whose participation in the war was recorded as of the very beginning of the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Are you aware that 10 December is the date when Pero Elez fatally wounded himself?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR PETKOVIC
utterances.text: I've heard of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: The Prosecution tenders 65 ter 17405 into evidence, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 17405 receives number P6812, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And the document no longer is needed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Mr. Petkovic, what was your role, if any, in the SDS leadership in Foca?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR PETKOVIC
utterances.text: I was an SDS member from day one. I didn't play any significant role. Since as a former athlete I knew a lot of people in Serbia and Montenegro, so I was asked to help the people with humanitarian aid. And when I say "the people," I mean Bosniaks, Muslims, and Croats. My role was to help them survive the hardships of the war, which is why I spent most of the time travelling for supplies and humanitarian aid in Serbia and Montenegro. As a result my record is 19 months in the war, that's what has been recorded under my name, as opposed to Pero Elez who was in the war from day one. There was a time when I had work obligation as a full-time professor at the school of medicine and dentistry.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Again, I please ask you to listen to the questions asked and just answer them so that we can keep on top of time. Were you a member of the Foca Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR PETKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: We briefly talked earlier about Ostojic, Cancar, Maksimovic, and Stanic. Now, these individuals, they attended meetings at your apartment in early 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR PETKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether that was a meeting of the Crisis Staff. I was friends with Maksimovic which is why I attended such meetings on several occasions, but I was never a member of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: My question was whether those individuals attended meetings at your apartment. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR PETKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm a bit hard of hearing. Could you please speak up.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Sure. You can also adjust the volume on your headsets.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, could the witness be assisted in doing so.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Did Maksimovic, Ostojic, Cancar, and Stanic attend meetings at your apartment in Foca in early 1992?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Maksimovic and Ostojic were refugees. They did come to my apartment, but not to any meetings. I was friends with Stanic who also visited me and vice versa. We were house friends, that was all. I don't understand what meetings you have in mind. We visited each other to have a drink together, to have a bite to eat, to have dinner or lunch together.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Mr. Petkovic, I will be more specific. I'm not talking about friendly visits where you would have a drink or beer or dinner. What I'm talking about is meetings specifically to talk about political organising of Serbs in Foca. Now, the reason I ask you this is that this Chamber has received evidence that these individuals attended meetings at your apartment to discuss such organisation.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And I refer the Chamber and the Defence to Exhibit P982, paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: So do you believe that that evidence is incorrect?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR PETKOVIC
utterances.text: This evidence is completely incorrect. I'm not sure that Velibor Ostojic ever came to visit me in my apartment.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in your statement at paragraph 5 you talk about Velecevo women's prison. You state that it was empty by April 20th, 1992, when the Crisis Staff moved in. Now you know that because you went to that prison around that time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: The Chamber has also heard evidence that you were at Velecevo late on the evening of 26 April 1992 along with Ostojic, Stanic, Maksimovic, Cancar, Milan Ivancic, and Stojan Blagojevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, the evidence I'm referring to, I can give you the citation in private session because it could reveal the identity of a protected witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's first hear the answer of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: The question is were you there, in fact, on that evening with those individuals, Mr. Petkovic?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR PETKOVIC
utterances.text: I was often there, but I don't know whether I was there on that evening. I can't answer. I can't remember the date. When you mentioned Ivancic, I remember that he was an officer. I don't know where he had come from. He spent some time in Foca but not very long. He had a rank but I don't know what rank, because I really didn't know much about those military matters. I'd never got involved in any of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: What was the reason that you would often go to the Velecevo prison, excuse me, specifically in April 1992?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR PETKOVIC
utterances.text: I was appointed to work in accordance with the function I had. I was the commander of the -- command of the headquarters. I was supposed to be there when I was not travelling on business and the business was fetching humanitarian aid. And since I was friends with Maksimovic and Miroslav Stanic before the war, obviously I was in touch with those friends. Maksimovic didn't have a vehicle. That's -- he often asked me to drive him from the city to Velecevo. Maksimovic even lived in my apartment for awhile, so I was appointed as commander of the headquarters administration.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Please listen specifically to my question. My understanding is that your appointment didn't occur until end of June or beginning of July. So I'm specifically talking about April 1992. During that period, other than acting as a driver to Maksimovic to take him to Velecevo, did you have any other duties or responsibilities that required you to be at Velecevo?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR PETKOVIC
utterances.text: I had no duties or responsibilities at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honours. I would like to point to paragraph 2 in the witness's statement which is relative to the period of time mentioned by the Prosecutor. It says here what was his duties given to him by the Crisis Staff when the conflict broke out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What's the objection now?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that the witness was misquoted. I believe that the witness said that he was engaged at the beginning of June to fetch humanitarian aid by the military, and before that that same duty was given to him by the Crisis Staff, and that was at the beginning of the conflict.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you give me page and line exactly where the misquote is? Where in the question is the witness quoted?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, on page 41, lines 12 through 17.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think Ms. MacGregor was not quoting the witness there. By the way, if that's your objection, the appropriate way of doing it is to say, objection, page so and so line that and that misrepresents the evidence. That's the way of doing it rather than to give the long explanations. But did you intend to quote? I do not see a quote, Ms. MacGregor.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: No, I was trying to focus in the witness's evidence on a specific date range.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And I believe when he was referring to his appointment, he was bringing it later in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's proceed. Perhaps you, keeping in the back of your mind what Mr. Stojanovic's concerns are, that you put the question or a similar question to the witness again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I have a question for the witness. Mr. Witness, again, at page 41, line 15 to 16, Madam MacGregor asks you: "... did you have any other duties or responsibilities that required you to be at Velecevo?" Your answer is: "I had no duties or responsibilities at all." But at page 41, line 3, you say: "I was appointed to work in accordance with the function I had. I was the commander of the -- command of the headquarters. I was supposed to be there," at the Velecevo prison, by the way, "when I was not travelling on business." Now, what were you supposed to be doing there at Velecevo when you were not travelling on business which contradicts what you said, you had no responsibilities there? Did you hear my question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: He's just waiting for the translation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me explain. Ms. Prosecutor asked me whether I participated in the Crisis Staff when I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No. I'm sorry, sir. I'm sorry, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And my --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you. Sorry, sir. Sorry. You said you were supposed to be there when you were not travelling on business. You also say you had no duties or responsibilities at all. Which of the two is correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was not tasked with anything by the Crisis Staff. The Crisis Staff didn't give me any duties or tasks. That's what I meant. My duty was to be the commander of the command administration and my obligation, which was my business, was to fetch humanitarian aid, to fetch supplies. I don't know what you're asking me. We are probably talking on cross purposes. I was not a member of the Crisis Staff. I don't know what I was supposed to be doing there. From the Crisis Staff, a message came to me via other people as to what I was supposed to be doing and where.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Again, I ask you to listen to my question. I haven't asked you anything about the Crisis Staff. You say and you were supposed to be at the Velecevo prison, female prison when you were not travelling on business. And I'm saying, if you were supposed to be there, what were you supposed to be doing there? Just all I'm asking.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just supposed to report there, that's all. I was not even supposed to be there. I was just there to report on my humanitarian work on my comings and goings to that end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Report to who?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I reported to the chief of logistics, Mr. Zelovic, because he was the one with whom I communicated the most.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed, Madam MacGregor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have nevertheless one or two follow-up questions. Chief of logistics of what exactly, Witness? Could you please -- you said you reported to the chief of logistics. Chief of logistics of what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was chief of logistics in charge of the warehouse where food and clothes were stored and from which it was distributed to the population. I used to call him "chief."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But was he a chief of logistics of a unit or of the Crisis Staff or -- I mean you describe what he did.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He also received tasks from the Crisis Staff to maintain this warehouse. He was in charge of it and we used to call him either administrator or chief or whatever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: He was appointed chief of logistics as you told us by the Crisis Staff. Is that what you say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Probably, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, probably is not --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know, but he probably was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, you emphasised that you had -- you had not received any tasks by the Crisis Staff. Paragraph 2 of your statement reads: "At the beginning of the conflict, the Crisis Staff tasked me with activities concerning ..." and then you explain what it is. A minute ago you say, "He was also tasked ..." and then you are referring to the chief of logistics. Do you have any explanation as to why in your statement we read that you were given this task by the Crisis Staff and where you, in your testimony today, you deny that you received tasks from the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I received from all those from the Crisis Staff, according to the situation. I cannot exactly explain to you how it worked. I would deliver humanitarian aid to the warden and that was part of a store house. He was definitely part of the Crisis Staff and the Crisis Staff was in charge. They would tell me where to go to seek assistance and obtain supplies for the people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, that leads me to the following question. You emphasised today during your testimony again and again that you were tasked with providing humanitarian aid to the people, to the population. In your statement, we read that you are tasked with activities concerning the supply of equipment and food to the population and units in Foca. Did you also supply food and equipment to units?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Whatever I received from the companies that I asked them to deliver, I received that and it was put in a joint store house that we shared with the Red Cross and from there they distributed it to the entire Foca population and probably they did the same for the units because the units also needed food and clothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. What they probably did is -- in your statement we read that you were "tasked with the supply of equipment and food to the population and units." If that's your explanation that probably this happened by others, then I have no follow-up questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Then I have a follow-up question. Units of what institution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those were allegedly units that had been mobilised by the Crisis Staff to defend and liberate the town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And what institution did those units belong to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, they belonged to the town itself, the Crisis Staff. I don't know how to put it. Somebody called them, whether it was the town Territorial Defence or whoever, I'm not exactly sure and I haven't sufficient knowledge about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
