utterances.text: I'm just not able to understand. Were they members of the Territorial Defence or were they units of the Crisis Staff? You say you don't know. They belonged to the Crisis Staff and then you say Territorial Defence. Can you repeat your answer, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know if you understand me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's why I'm asking you the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The units that were engaged at the time, as well as combatants that were engaged on the front line, received food and equipment. The same was done for the population of the town. So for everyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Stop there, stop there. These combatants, what institution did they belong to, these units of combatants?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, how shall I put it, they belonged to the entire town, and the Crisis Staff was in command of them. I don't know how to explain to you to whom they belonged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. MacGregor, could you tell us, we are about to take a break, how much time you'd need after the break?

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: I actually have two very discreet questions related to Velecevo prison and then I'm finished. It may make sense to do them before the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But, of course, that needs the consent of the -- at least I want to consult the Defence. Two more questions, Mr. Stojanovic, before the break, would that -- otherwise we take the break now?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's agreeable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. MacGregor, two questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: The witness who provided evidence about Velecevo prison also stated that you were in a room -- excuse me, that there were -- that the prison was equipped to communicate with other posts with a Motorola and with telephone lines. Did you observe those devices there when you went to the prison?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR PETKOVIC
utterances.text: No. I know that not even some of the combatants -- combatants didn't have Motorola radios and there was no way that they had them in the prison. Even all telephone lines were down as a result of power cuts.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: My question was only if you observed them and your answer was that you didn't. My final question --

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR PETKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: -- the chief of logistics that you referred to, Zelovic, was his first name Cedo?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: The Prosecution has no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. MacGregor. We'll take a break. Could you give an estimate, Mr. Stojanovic, as to how much time you'd need after the break?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Up to ten minutes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we take a break but not until after the witness has left the courtroom. We'd like to see you back in 20 minutes from now, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We resume at 25 minutes past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. MacGregor, you offered to give us in private session a reference. The Chamber can do without at this moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If it is -- if you would just give a P number of -- I mean, P numbers are not confidential, are they, and then we always have an opportunity to check it. As I did with the previous one, I can check it right away. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Shall I do that now, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you give the P number then that's -- we don't need anything else.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: The exhibit number is P2935.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then Mr. Stojanovic, any further questions for the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a few questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, to an answer by the Prosecutor, you -- to a question by the Prosecutor, you talked about the prison at Velecevo. Until when was the Crisis Staff accommodated in the facility of the female prison at Velecevo?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR PETKOVIC
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff arrived there around the 15th or 20th of April. It occupied the premises of the former female prison which was empty. There was just a janitor there or a couple of janitors who maintained the premises. And I know that the Crisis Staff was there until the moment the brigades were established and until the moment the artillery tactical group was set up. And after that, I don't know what happened, how much longer they remained in that facility.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were asked whether you saw a Motorola. Do you know anything about the range of that radio set which is known under the name Motorola?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Approximately 500 to a thousand metre, I believe, but I don't know. I'm sure that there weren't any there at the moment. Telephone lines were down. The only telephone lines that were working were those within the city network. We did not have any connection with the outside world. If somebody wanted to communicate with anybody, they had to go to Montenegro in order to talk to their families who had fled the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Were roads passable during that period of time in May, June, July 1992? Could you take a road from Foca across the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina to Pale or Sokolac?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR PETKOVIC
utterances.text: No. Only from Montenegro could you do that, either across Plevlje or Scepan Polje. That was the only way to reach Foca.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And now let me ask you why one could not take the main road towards Pale and Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Muslim units had blocked the road towards Gorazde and towards Kalinovik and Sarajevo. Muslim units had barricaded the rest of the town. Our units were on the borders of those territories.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Petkovic. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Moloto has one or more questions for you. I apologise, Judge Fluegge has one or more questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Just a question with respect to your background. In paragraph 1 of your statement, you tell us that you were a teacher at the secondary school centre in Foca. What was your specialty? What did you teach?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR PETKOVIC
utterances.text: I was a physical training teacher until 1993 when I moved to the medical faculty, and I worked there for 13 years until I retired.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: What did you teach there at the faculty of dental medicine?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR PETKOVIC
utterances.text: The same subject, physical training, physical education.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any further questions, Ms. MacGregor? Mr. Petkovic, this concludes your evidence. Thank you for having come to The Hague and for having answered all the questions whether put to you by the Prosecution or by the Defence or by the Bench. I wish you a safe return home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, the Chamber received meanwhile a list of associated exhibits for Witness Sarenac. If my math is okay, I see still 22 items on that list. Are there any objections from the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. If I may, and thank you for this opportunity, the Prosecution would like to just provide a brief response and maybe clarify the question that Your Honours just had with respect to the exhibits. May I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: On 24 September, 2014, the Defence filed an urgent motion seeking to add 22 documents to its 65 ter exhibit list. The documents at issue relate to the statement of Witness Desimir Sarenac. The motion was filed during the testimony of the witness. As a preliminary matter, the Prosecution notes that 20, not 22, of the 65 ter numbers listed in annex A of the motion are not referenced as part of the Defence Exhibit list, the exceptions being 65 ter number 1D04399, which is already a part of the Defence 65 ter exhibit list, and 65 ter 1D03057 which is described on the Defence exhibit list as a different set of materials relating to a photo analysis. It is unclear to the Prosecution what exhibit -- it was unclear to the Prosecution what exhibit is properly associated to the 65 ter number due to the use of the same 65 ter number for a 1st Smbr information report dated 13 August 1993. Currently we also do not know the content of the photo analysis and whether it is intended for use by the Defence. The parties did discuss this and for the time being the parties have agreed to use 65 ter number 1D03057 for the 13 August 1993 1st Smbr information report and will further discuss the fate of the photo analysis. With this being said, the Defence submits in paragraph 5 of the motion that there is good cause to add the documents. The Prosecution disagrees. The motion was not filed in the timely manner and the documents were previously part of the witness's Karadzic materials. As such, it is the Prosecution's position that the Defence should have included the documents on its exhibit list when it decided to list Mr. Sarenac as a witness or at the very least promptly sought their addition once the Defence completed the current statement of the witness on 27 July 2014. Notwithstanding what we submit to be a lack of good cause, the Prosecution does not oppose the addition of the remaining 21 documents due to the minimal prejudice this caused to us during our preparations considering the length and amount of material and the time before the testimony of the witness. Should the Chamber allow the addition of the documents, the Prosecution also discussed this with the Defence and we would appreciate it if the Defence could file a written submission similar to the one that they did for Witness GRM246. This would allow the Prosecution to properly articulate its views on each of the respective materials in a written response. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you still want to make up your mind as far as admission is concerned if we would allow the documents to be added to the 65 ter list?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes, but more importantly articulate our specific views on the documents in a written submission, I think. Due to the nature of the documents, we would like to approach that in writing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but then in view of a decision whether or not to admit. Yes. One second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, could I hear the position of the Defence in relation to what Mr. Weber just raised.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. I did discuss with my learned friend just before this session on all these topics, and I actually had different understanding that they do not oppose to the admission of the documents but -- actually to the adding the documents to the 65 ter list, and they don't -- do want our written submission regarding the admission of the documents and we are ready to do that if, of course, the documents are added on our 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Weber, I take it that this doesn't need any further response.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the Chamber grants the request to add the documents to the 65 ter list. I'll not list them all because the next step is that you're invited to make a written submission so that Mr. Weber will have an opportunity to respond to that before the Chamber decides on admission and it will become clear from that list what was added to the 65 ter list and what was granted leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps it's the other way around, but let's be very practical. Mr. Weber is smiling as well so it's -- he's very practical. Could we then receive that, one would say, within a week?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, it's feasible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then leave is granted and we are waiting for the submissions by the -- written submissions by the Defence in relation to the associated exhibits for the witness statement of Mr. Sarenac. Any other matter? I'm not aware of any. This means that we adjourn. We have a non-sitting week next week. We are not sitting tomorrow, which means that we will resume on Monday, the 13th of October, 9.30 in the morning, and I think we will be back in courtroom I. We stand adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
